The Ant-eating Chat (Myrmecocichla formicivora) is a medium-sized passerine endemic to southern Africa, where it inhabits open savanna and grassland. As is typical for altricial songbirds, newly hatched nestlings emerge at a remarkably small body size, with the neonatal wet weight averaging a mere 4.4 grams [Wwb = 4.4 grams]. This initial mass is quite modest relative to the species' ultimate adult body weight, highlighting the substantial growth trajectory that must be completed during the nestling period. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of incubation within a shaded ground burrow, which are maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the incubation period culminates in hatching after an average of 14.5 days [ab = 14.5 days]. This developmental interval, measured from egg-laying to emergence of the altricial young, is consistent with the duration observed in other open-country passerines of analogous body size. The transition from dependence on yolk reserves to the onset of exogenous feeding marks a critical nutritional shift in the chick's early life history.

Once hatched, the altricial chicks experience a period of rapid somatic growth inside the nest cavity, entirely dependent on biparental provisioning. The developmental progression follows a predictable sequence under the elevated body temperatures typical of an active, metabolically active nestling, which are maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. At this thermal state, the fledging event, defined as the chick's first sustained flight and departure from the nest, occurs at 17 days since birth [tx = 17 days since birth] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively brief nestling period places the species among passerines with a moderately accelerated developmental schedule, likely an adaptation to reduce predation risk in open habitats. Puberty is reached at 51 days since birth [tp = 51 days since birth] under the same thermal regime, indicating that substantial physiological and morphological development must occur before reproductive competence is achieved at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The achievement of flight feathers and coordinated motor skills at this juncture enables the fledgling to evade terrestrial predators, though it remains partially dependent on adult birds for food during the initial weeks following nest departure. The subsequent attainment of nutritional independence marks the beginning of the free-living juvenile phase.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs after a more protracted interval of somatic growth and behavioral development. The age at which an individual produces its first brood is 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], a point considerably deferred beyond pubertal onset at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay between physiological maturity and first reproduction is a common life-history pattern in passerines, often linked to the time required to acquire a breeding territory, establish a pair bond, and gain sufficient foraging experience to sustain the energetic demands of egg production and chick rearing. The first successful breeding event typically occurs only after an individual has secured a stable territory and formed a durable pair bond, conditions that may not be met until the second calendar year of life in many individuals inhabiting suboptimal habitat patches.

Adult body mass stabilizes after the first year, with the ultimate wet weight in fully grown, breeding birds reaching 46 grams [Wwi = 46 grams]. This asymptotic mass is approximately an order of magnitude greater than the neonatal weight, underscoring the substantial investment in growth during the first few months of life. Reproductive output is constrained by both the small clutch size and the limited frequency of breeding attempts within a single season. Females lay between 3 and 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 3 and 5 eggs per clutch], and typically produce only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This low annual fecundity, combined with the moderate adult body mass, aligns with a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival and protracted territorial occupancy over high immediate reproductive output. Such a strategy is often characteristic of arid-zone species facing unpredictable food resources, where the energetic costs of repeated breeding attempts may compromise adult survivorship.

Longevity records for the Ant-eating Chat indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] in the wild, a duration that is comparatively high among passerines of its body size at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This substantial potential for long-term survival, when coupled with the low annual reproductive rate, places the species firmly on the slow end of the life-history continuum. The total number of offspring produced over a lifetime is therefore constrained by both the small clutch size and the single annual breeding event. The life-history strategy of this species, emphasizing adult persistence and modest reproductive output, is well-suited to the variable and resource-limited environments of southern African savannas where it has evolved.
